intro: “Bittendes Kind” (Pleading Child) is No. 4 of Kinderszenen, Op. 15. The piece is seventeen bars long and ends on an A-seventh chord.

sections.label: Coda · Ends on an A-seventh chord

cues.title: Opening phrase, bars 1–4
cues.text: The melody leaps up from B and falls back through G–F♯–E. Semiquavers fill the spaces beneath it, and the bass rests after each note. The two-bar phrase is played twice, first piano and then pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 7, bars 1–4; notes confirmed in Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=366
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Presentation copy for Liszt, 1839
cues.text: In Vienna on 13 March 1839 Schumann inscribed an early copy of Kinderszenen “to F. Liszt in friendship”. Above Pleading Child he added a tempo direction by hand: Langsam (slowly).
cues.evidence: Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 7: Schumann’s inscription and handwritten tempo direction in the presentation copy for Liszt. Translation from the German. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

cues.title: Final chord, bar 17
cues.text: The piece ends in bar 17 on a dominant seventh chord, A–C♯–E–G, held under a fermata. The chord does not resolve to D.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 7, bar 17: A-seventh chord and fermata; pitches confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: A second phrase over D
transitions.how: The first phrase ends on A major harmony. A new phrase begins with C♮ over a repeated D in the bass, and E♭ and B♭ appear in the accompanying semiquavers. Schumann marks it piano, then repeats it pianissimo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 7, bars 4–8; melody, bass and accidentals confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: Melody rises over a B bass
transitions.how: The bass moves from D to B. Above it the melody rises F♯–G♯–A–B, reaches C♯ and then falls to A. This two-bar phrase is marked ritardando. Schumann repeats the phrase with the same ritardando, in bars 9 and 11 of the Breitkopf & Härtel first edition.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 7, bars 9–12: ritardando in bars 9 and 11; bass begins on B.

transitions.title: Return of the opening phrase
transitions.how: The rising phrase settles on A major harmony. The bass drops to a lower A and resumes its separated notes, and above them the opening leap from B to G returns. Bars 1–4 are repeated, with a further ritardando in the final repetition.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 7, bars 12–16; return of bars 1–4 and final ritardando.

transitions.title: A fermata on the dominant
transitions.to: Coda · Ends on an A-seventh chord
transitions.how: The last ritardando leads to a low A, with C♯ and E in the middle and G above. Schumann holds this dominant seventh under a fermata, and the piece ends without resolving it. The next piece, Happy Enough, is in D major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 7–8: the A-seventh ending of No. 4 is followed by No. 5 in D major.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
